(2.1.83) Thus, having honored her in this manner, if one asks how one should offer oblations into her mouth, he says: "Having recited once, one should give once," and so forth. "Once" means at one time; having uttered each mantra individually, one should offer each individual oblation. One should not, however, offer a hundred oblations with a single mantra uttered all at once. Even while offering in this way, if one asks how many [oblations] should be offered for each, he says: "But having taken seven more," and so forth.

Because it is relative (*sāpekṣatva*), the word "additional" (*adhika*) brings to mind the number three from the immediately preceding set of fire-oblations (*vahnihoma*). One should offer ten plus seven—that is, seventeen—of each substance. Among the substances mentioned in the stated number, one should perform a "totalization" (*saṃpiṇḍikā*, *saṃpiṇḍā*) even of those that have been offered, extending up to ten thousand (*ayuta*) or a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).
\paragraph{2.1.84} \textbf{The Procedure by Means of Oblation (*āhuti*)}
Regarding the reading *vṛttam* (MS\pcorr) instead of *vṛttim* (MS\acorr):
[the phrase] "elevated, remaining from the oblation, intent upon the cause" means "intent upon the purpose of the oblation. Having aimed at that, there is peace.
Peace. (Note: *śāntiṃ* is an emendation for *śānti*)

Having directed one's mind toward nourishment, malevolent magic, or the accomplishment of one's own or another's aims, and having uttered [the mantra] with speech, one steps far away, bypassing the sequence, and says: "With a vessel full of ghee," and so forth.
The master of the sacrifice should cause the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered with a vessel filled with ghee vomited forth from his ears.
Regarding the remainder of the full oblation, one might ask: "Will that Blessed Lady remain in the sacrificial pit itself?"
"He will stand."

If he says "by activity," [it refers to] the passage beginning with *hutavṛtta*. That is, when the *huti* (oblation) has been performed (*nirvṛtta*). Regarding the word "of the gods" (*devānām*), that goddess dissolves into her own body; she becomes absorbed within the body of the yogin.

2.1.85–86. Regarding the phrase "when all the oblations are complete" (*sampūrṇṇasarva-m-āhutye*): this means when the entire offering of oblations has been completed. Regarding the phrase "with the mantra-seal complete" (*pūrṇṇamantramudrake*): when the oblation has been offered with the complete mantra-seal, one might ask, "How does she dissolve as she dissolves? To this he says: "By the power of the breath," and so forth (86b). By the power of the breath, having drawn her into his own body, the wise yogi should meditate upon her in the form of himself.

2.1.87. If one asks what should be done with whatever remains of the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, he says: "The remainder, having offered with three [oblations]," and so forth. One should swiftly offer it into the mouth of the fire-deity, which has been manifested by means of three oblations. If one asks whether the fire will remain or depart once the rite of *homa* has concluded, he says: "By means of the offerings and the presentation of the *bali*," and so forth. Then, one should dismiss the fire after performing the worship and offering of the *bali* with its respective mantra and mudrā.
Unbroken grains of śāli rice.

[The materials include] awnless *śāli* rice, white sesame, white mustard, and wheat seeds; [the wood of] the *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *parkaṭī*, and mango—these fourteen finger-breadths in length—and the five milky trees, [to be used] with ghee and milk. "But it is to be drunk with milk," [it is said]; [this refers to] honey.

For pacification (*śānti*), the substances are milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and grains such as black sesame, black beans (*māṣa*), and red rice; likewise, the five milky trees with branches ten finger-breadths long, smeared with ghee, honey, saffron, and milk, as well as milk-rice with ghee, are used for nourishment (*puṣṭi*). For subjugation (*vaśya*), red and black sesame, *priyaṅgu*, *nāgakeśara*, *aśurī*, and *śatapuṣpa* fruits, along with the wood of *devadāru*, *vaṭa*, *vāsaka*, and *nāgakeśara* twelve finger-breadths long, mixed with honey and clarified butter, are employed.
2.1.95–96: Black sesame, black *māṣa* beans, *bhallātaka*, and *ariṣṭa*; the wood of *kālakubja* and *bhallātaka*—these, with blood-mixed pungent oil, are used for malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*).

2.1.97–98: Mustard seeds, *muḍga* beans, *māṣa* beans, and road-dust; the wood of *dhuttūraka* and *vāsaka*—these, in a fire of blood-mixed pungent oil, are used for eradication (*uccāṭana*). 2.1.99–100: Fish...

Meat, gold, and rice grains mixed with crow feathers.

For the attainment of sovereignty: the *śrīphala* fruit, curd, honey, and an *aśvattha* tree sprout smeared with ghee.

The disciples—those who are devoted to the sacrificial altar, yoga, and meditation; intent on hearing and reciting the scriptures; constantly devoted to their gurus; delighting in giving; abstaining from sensual pleasures; free from anger; devoid of egoism; not indolent; and not harsh in speech—are [to be accepted] by the teachers.
[The following should be performed] by the teachers:
[the punishment of] those who revile the teachers, gurus, and deities, those of cruel mind, and the evil-souled.

"I have a curiosity regarding what is called *jalahoma* (water-oblation); may the Blessed One explain that.

Thereupon the Blessed One said: "Listen, O Vajra, according to reality," and so forth. "According to reality" means according to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). "And indeed, spread out like a canopy" refers to a certain reservoir of water.

Having repeatedly recited the root mantra, "Oṃ jrūṃ hūṃ svāhā," one should strike the crown of the goddess; thus one should perform the sacrifice.

2.2.23 He states the number of recitations: "By ten thousand [recitations] for the rite," and so forth. The All-Knowing One has said that by offering ten thousand oblations of white flowers, the life of the patient increases.
2.2.24 Peace for the household is attained by offering ten thousand oblations of milk with *karavīra* red flowers.
2.2.25 Peace for the village is attained by offering ten thousand oblations of milk with *nāgakeśara* flowers.
2.2.26 For the peace of kingdoms, cities, villages, and so forth, the lotus (*padma*) is the ritual effective for all purposes (*sārvakarmika*).

2.2.27 One should offer oblations of priyaṅgu, bilva, utpala, and kumuda flowers, one by one, for the sake of sovereignty and for the destruction of enemy kingdoms. Furthermore, by drinking a mouthful of milk or water while reciting this root mantra, there is nourishment of the body.
Thus ends the second chapter on the *parapīṭha* in the *Mitapadā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) composed by the illustrious Durjayacandra. ॐ.

2.3.1 Having explained the second chapter, he speaks in order to explain the third chapter, beginning with "Listen, O Vajra," and so forth. O Vajrapāṇi, by virtue of being the sovereign of the maṇḍala circle...
[37 recto] Or, O Great King, [he is called Mahārāja] because he has been turned [toward sovereignty], or because of his lordship over the yakṣas.
The Great King [emended from "the Great King"]

He states the object of the act of hearing: "the characteristic of the further shore of saṃsāra. Saṃsāra consists of birth, old age, death, and so forth. Regarding this, it has been said in some places:
The triad of origination, maintenance, and dissolution is proclaimed as existence (bhava).
...is proclaimed as surely [the case].

Thus: its "other shore" is its cessation; its cause is that which is characterized by the further shore of *saṃsāra*. He states its qualification: **free from existence and non-existence**. Existence and non-existence refer to eternalism (*śāśvata*) and nihilism (*uccheda*); it is devoid of these two, hence **free from existence and non-existence**. **One should avoid both the pure and the impure**: the pure is dispassion (*virāga*), while the impure is passion (*rāga*); one should avoid even those two. If one asks why, he says: **beginning with "today" and ending with "in the perception of phenomena"**, and so forth.
[The term] *saṃjñā* and so forth [means]:

being devoid of dual existence, it is non-duality (*advaitā*), the state of non-duality (*advaitatā*). The "perception of phenomena" (*dharmasaṃjñā*) is the conceptualizing of phenomena; the sense is that while this exists, how could there be this duality of purity, impurity, and so forth? Now, one might object: even if non-duality were established, this dual mode of existence would cease, yet non-duality itself is not established.
Is it "na sidhyate" (is not established) or "sidhyate" (is established)?

Since there exist objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) such as form (*rūpa*), sound, and so forth, and there exist apprehending faculties (*grāhaka*) such as the eye and the other sense organs, one might suspect that the twofold division of entities into the apprehended and the apprehender does not cease to exist. Anticipating this objection, he provides a refutation with reference to form, beginning with the words: "Form is empty of the beginning and the end," and so on. Because the cause for its arising is non-existent, form is empty at the beginning due to its non-arising; because that which has not arisen does not persist even at the conclusion, it is also empty at the end.
The same applies to sound, smell, taste, touch, and the rest.

If one asks, "Since all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty from beginning to end, and since form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are themselves empty, where will this non-duality (*advaitatā*) abide? he says: "But it is established in the middle" (*madhye tu samavasthitam*). In the middle—that is, in the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), characterized by the absence of duality, consisting of the mind’s non-alienated nature, and resembling the reflection of the moon in water—it is "established"; thus, this [non-duality] is established. The word "but" (*tu*) shows that, furthermore, this non-duality is indeed proven in this manner.

2.3.3 If it is asked what the characteristic of that Blessed Lady, the Middle Way, is— wherein this non-duality of the established [reality] resides— the author states its characteristic: "non-empty" (aśūnya).

"But the middle" means: it is non-empty by virtue of being the object of perception, and it is empty by virtue of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which consists of these two natures is the middle. Regarding the alternative reading, "the impure and the pure are the middle": therein, every entity is impure due to the defilement of the stains of subject and object; the non-entity is pure because it is devoid of both of these. The middle is either the unity or the avoidance of these two. If one asks how such a thing is established, he says:

"By means of the vision of equality alone," and so forth. "Equality" (*samatā*) refers to the sameness, by virtue of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), even between Mount Sumeru and a single atom (*paramāṇu*). Of that...
of that, surely.
Observation is the vision of equality; by that alone is success achieved.

It is established (*sidhyati*). Furthermore, if one asks what that [Middle Way] is like, he says: "That which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated," and so forth. "To be cultivated" means that which is not to be abandoned; "not to be cultivated" means that which is not to be adopted. Thus...
[38 recto] Thus.

The meaning is that it is neither to be abandoned nor to be adopted. Regarding the phrase "arising from equal cognition" (*samajñānasamudbhavam*): "arising" (*samudbhavam*) means produced or manifested.

If one asks, "What would be the purpose of this?", he states the purpose with the words beginning "of those whose bodies are situated in equality" (*samasthitadehānām*). "Equal" (*samam*) refers to equanimity. This refers to the observation of internal aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and so forth, as being equal to external objects such as forms, sounds, and the like.
Those whose vision and intellect [are such], they are those whose vision is the view of equality (*samadarśanadṛṣṭi*).
[The views] (°dṛṣṭayas) [MSpcorr, °dṛṣṭayaḥ MSacorr]

"For those yogins" [refers to] "the arising of equal knowledge. Equal knowledge is the non-differentiation between cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. The sense is: what is the use of saying more?

If equal knowledge arises through the vision of equal seeing, then Vajrapāṇi, desiring to know that knowledge, said: "I wish to hear," and so forth. "But what is equal seeing like? Regarding an object that is divided into the three categories of pure, impure, and neither—how then does this equal seeing of one who is non-dualistic [arise]?

"But as for the *dharma*": among the phenomena (*dharmas*) appearing in a state of duality, the *dharma* is non-duality (*advaita*). Regarding the question, "How are they to be known by their own nature?", that is, "How are these mutually contradictory phenomena to be known as having a single identical nature?"—in response to Vajrapāṇi’s question, the Blessed One said: "Listen, O Vajra, according to reality."
O Vajra, O Vajrapāṇi, listen to how it truly is, according to its own nature; I shall tell it to you: non-dual gnosis is the defining characteristic.
Regarding the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): it is the characteristic of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), and it is the cause for the realization of non-dual gnosis.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is devoid of dual existence" (*varjitadvayabhāvasya*): it is devoid of a twofold state; therein, "twofold" (*dvaidha*) refers to the two, namely the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). That very existence is "dual-existence" (*dvayabhāva*); it is "devoid of" or "free from" that dual-existence. Regarding the phrase "non-dual for those who know the Dharma" (*advayā dharmajñāninām*): "non-dual" means not twofold. "For those who know the Dharma"—this [is the meaning].
Thus it is said.

That is the non-dual knowledge of phenomena (*advayadharmajñāna*). Because of conviction, he speaks subsequently regarding the vision that is preceded by and followed by the Dharma: "By means of the three purities," and so forth. "By the three" means in a threefold manner. "Purity" refers to the complete purification of all phenomena. "All yogas and so forth at the beginning" refers to the yoga of the deity and so on.
First:

"Pure by nature" means that the nature of phenomena is the absence of a nature possessing the three characteristics; because it is indivisible, it is pure, the Body-Vajra. The mind, which is unarisen, non-referential, indivisible, and appearing as space, is the Mind-Vajra.

The mind-vajra is indeed the yoga that is the conjunction of mantras. By means of that yoga, which is like the sound of an echo, the pure one is the Vajra of Speech, purified by yoga; such is its very nature.
% [svabhāva°] MS\pcorr, svabhāvā MS\acorr%
"All phenomena are pure, purified by the vajra; they are purified by yoga. Thus, 'I am pure'—such is this even-mindedness.
(2.3.10) Having recited these three purities, what kind [of result] is it? It brings about the accomplishment of the union with the deity of the auspicious state. Immediately thereafter...
Regarding the phrase "immediately after this very [act]," it means immediately after purification (*śuddhi*).
Immediately thereafter.
One should perform the yoga of the deity.

He states the location for performing that [practice]: "In a place agreeable to the mind," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and with a canopy spread out": it refers to a specific location characterized by a wide-spreading canopy and the like.

2.3.12–15. Regarding the phrase "on all sides by means of the ten positions": this refers to the eight directions beginning with the east, as well as below and above, because of their being scattered [therein].

On all sides, in the ten locations adorned with circles of fragrant jewels, [the procedure] is performed according to what was stated in the first chapter of the *Parapīṭhīya* beginning with the words "The calculation of the limbs" (*kalanam aṅgāni*).

Having sequentially emanated oneself as Jñānaḍākinī, one should perform the worship of oneself. Immediately thereafter, in the space-element, upon the maṇḍalas of the four elements arising from *yuṃ*, *kṣuṃ*, *suṃ*, and *huṃ*, and upon Mount Sumeru arising from *suṃ* which contains a pair of *hūṃ*s; in the five locations—the center and the four directions starting with the east and north—of the vajra produced by the *hūṃ* visualized in the upturned left hand—one should join [the hands] with the syllable *hūṃ*. Striking [with the vajra] preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ*, together with the half-anger (*sārddhakrodha*).

The gift that destroys malice purifies the seven netherworlds. This is the mantra for the Vajrabhūmi mudrā. There, upon the vajra-ground, [it is said]: "covered by the four colors and so forth. Having visualized Vairocana upon a lotus and moon with the *praṇava* (oṃ) syllable as his wheel, one should visualize him endowed with those same four colors: white, yellow, red, and black. Regarding the phrase "arisen from a golden house" (*kāñcanāgārasaṃbhūtam*): a golden house is a *kāñcanāgāra*; the meaning is that a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) fashioned of gold has manifested.

"Adorned with the seven precious gems" means that it is surrounded on all sides by the seven [gems]: moonstone (*candrakānta*), sunstone (*sūryakānta*), sapphire (*indranīla*), topaz (*puṣparāga*), ruby (*padmarāga*), ... [and so forth].
"Adorned with nets of tinkling bells (*kiṅkinījālamāla*) inlaid with rubies and lapis lazuli," refers to the pillars of the archway (*toraṇadaṇḍa*).
[The reading °daṇḍa° is supported by the corrected version of the manuscript (MS\pcorr), while °diṇḍa° is the uncorrected reading of the manuscript (MS\acorr).]
Clinging to the fluttering banners of pride raised by the deer [of the senses], it resounded.
Minor [offenses]

Regarding the phrase "an expanse according to one's own desire" (*svecchavistaram*): it means as much as is possible, rather than a fixed measurement such as three or four cubits. Having constructed the vajra-fence, canopy, and so forth by means of the mantras and mudrās described in the first chapter on the *parapīṭha*, beginning with "having made two fists," he speaks in order to display the *samayamudrā*—the foremost of all mudrās—within the mantras for the "downpour of rain" and so on, for the wheel of deities such as the Jñānaḍākinīs who have been installed in their respective places.
"Vajramuṣṭi," and so forth: one [should place] the two vajra-fists on the breast at Vindhya.

Like a vajra because of its indestructibility, having placed the left vajra-fist at the heart, [he says] "kakṣikā"; the *kakṣikā* is the index finger raised upward from the fist. Therein, one should lift up and raise the right fist.

2.3.18 Having explained the mudrā, he speaks in order to extract the mantra: "Just as the vajra-like," and so forth. Just as the five Buddhas, who are well-known as vajras, are themselves the vajra-like seed-syllable, the syllable *hūṃ*. "Offered with obeisance nearby" means beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*. "Of this" refers to the mantra of this mudrā, which is *yaṃ*. "Likewise, showing the pledge" means one should display this root mudrā accompanied by this mantra.

2.3.18. Where this mudrā is to be displayed, he describes their seats: "The lion-seat is indeed fivefold," and so forth. One should visualize five lions upon the sun, beneath the white parasol, in the four cardinal directions starting from the east, with the fifth in the center.

2.3.20–21 ff. Therein, one should meditate upon oneself as Jñānaḍākinī—arisen from the sign of one’s own mantra through the empowerment of one’s own breath—having three faces and six arms, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, with hair disheveled like a mass of pearls, distinguished by attributes such as being blue and so forth, while seated in the center. This is according to the detailed [explanation] in the *Jñānaḍākinī-abhisamaya*, which consists of twelve thousand [verses].

In the chamber of the *yogāmbara* [tantra] held [therein], these [deities] beginning with Vajraḍākinī are to be described; since their colors and emblems will become manifest in that very [text], they are not mentioned here.
What are these texts?

2.3.53 Regarding what was not stated there, it is said here: "In front of these, such as the *bimba*," and so forth. This means in front of, that is, before, these *bimba*s of the deities of the maṇḍala. "And also the commitment (*samaya*)" means that one should display whatever mantra and mudrā constitute one's own specific commitment (*svasamaya*).

2.3.54–56ab. In this context, having set aside the mantra of Jñānaḍākinī extracted in the first chapter, [the author] states the mantra of Vajraḍāka and the others, beginning with *svarapūrvādibījasya*. The vowels (*svarāḥ*) are fifteen; that which has these as its preceding part is "preceded by vowels" (*svarapūrva*), namely the syllable *aḥ*.
That alone is the single remaining vowel among [the vowels] beginning with *ā*.

The mantra of the four goddesses of the directions begins with the seed-syllables preceded by the vowels. If one asks what that [mantra] is like, it says: "Praṇamā huta antima," and so forth. *Praṇamā* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ). *Huta* is *svāhā*. This *aḥ*-kāra, which stands at the beginning and end of this, is the mantra of Vajraḍākinī, independent of any other vowels.

2.3.56cd–57ab. If it is asked: "Just as this seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of the undifferentiated *vajra*-syllables, what is the case for the others, such as the *ghora*-syllables and so forth? he says: "In the second [consonant] of the vowel-group," and so on. A group of vowels is a "vowel-group" (*svaravarga*). Vowels... [MS\pcorr, svaravarggaḥ svaravarggaḥ MS\acorr]... [MS\pcorr, svaravarggaḥ !svara°] MS\acorr].

The pair of pairs: *a-ā*, *i-ī*, and so forth. Therein, within the group of initial vowels, the second vowel is the letter *ā*. Its constituent part is this final vowel, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Ghorī.
What is its function?
Regarding the phrase "of this [mantra] employed with its seed-syllable" (*asya bījaprayuktasya*), it refers to what follows immediately after this.

One should place or establish the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*) like a staff beside the employed seed-syllable *ghorī*; however, one should not [place] two dots (*bindu*), for those are subsequently erased.
If it is asked, "What is the use of wiping that away?", he says: "It would be the seed-syllable of Vetālī."

Regarding the phrase "of this seed-mantra when employed" (asya bīja-prayuktasya): for the sake of accomplishing the seed-mantra of Caṇḍālī, one should place an *anusvāra* dot (*bindu*) above the head of that vowel which has two lost dots (*luptabindudvaya*), that is, above its form; thus the seed-mantra of Caṇḍālī is accomplished.

2.3.59cd–60ab: Having stated the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the goddesses of the directions, he states the seed-syllables of the four goddesses of the corners with the words “*napuṃsā pūrvabījasye*,” etc. “*Napuṃsā*”: the neuter vowels—namely the four ending with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Among these, the first is the vowel *ṛ*; that is the seed-syllable of Siṃhinī. 2.3.60cd–63ab: In this same manner, the remaining three seed-syllables belong respectively to Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Ulūkī.

\paragraph{2.3.63cd–64} Having stated the seed-syllables of the nine *cakravartinīs*, he speaks in order to state the seed-syllables of the four gate-guardians, beginning with "Of the fifth group," and so forth. The fifth group is the labial group (*pavarga*). Its second [letter] is the phoneme *pha*. Regarding "the root-sound" (*mūlanāda*): according to the convention of the Dharma, the root is the vowel *u*; the sound (*nāda*) arising from the drop (*bindu*) is the vowel *a*. Joined below and above these two is the mantra of *Ḍākinī*.

\paragraph{2.3.65} Regarding the phrase "joined with the letter *e* and the *bindu*": the letter *e* is the eleventh vowel; the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. By means of these two, that very syllable *pha* is to be joined; this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *Dīpinī*.

\paragraph{2.3.66} Regarding the phrase "with the letter *o* and the *bindu*": one should join that same syllable with the letter *o* conjoined with the *bindu*. This would be the seed-syllable of the *Cūṣiṇī*.
\paragraph{2.3.67} Regarding the phrase "the letter *ra*, the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *bindu*": the term "goad" (*aṅkuśa*) refers to the letter *i*.
The footnote states: "Repha, aṅkuśa, and bindu. Here, *repha* refers to the letter *ra*, and *aṅkuśa* refers to the vowel *i*. Thus, it means *repha*, *aṅkuśa*, and the vowel *i*.
Thus [ends the section on] the syllable *ṛ*.

One should join that very syllable with the letter *ri* and the bindu; this is the seed-syllable of Kambojī. Since it has been explained in one place, the *praṇama* and *āhutaka* gestures are not explained at every step.

[2.3.68] Now, he describes the mudrās accordingly, beginning with "both fists," and so forth. The Jñānaḍākinī mudrā consists of the two hands firmly clenched into fists, with the tips of the two middle fingers extended and their tips touching as shown.
2.3.69 The touching and moving of the two middle fingers with the two thumbs of hands joined together is the *vajraḍākī-mudrā*.
2.3.70 Regarding the term *samau*: the spreading of the two thumbs from fists firmly clenched together is the *ghorī-mudrā*.
2.3.71 Regarding the word *atra*: the spreading of the two little fingers of this same mudrā is the *vettālī-mudrā*.
2.3.72 Regarding the term *atra*: furthermore, the spreading of the two middle fingers of this firmly bound mudrā is the Caṇḍālī-mudrā.

2.3.73 Having explained the four mudrās of the goddesses of the directions, he states the mudrās of the goddesses of the corners: "The two vajra-fists," and so forth. The spreading of the two index fingers with their tips touching, from the two firmly bound vajra-fists, is the mudrā for the four corner goddesses beginning with Siṃhī.
2.3.74 With the face [downward], the two hands cast downward into the mouth while the syllable *hūṃ* is being uttered is the Ḍākinī-mudrā.
2.3.75 The *dīpinī-mudrā* consists of placing the hands in a hollowed *añjali* gesture upon the head, which is beautiful due to the utterance of the *praṇava*.
2.3.76 The *cūṣiṇī-mudrā* is established by placing the hollowed *añjali* in a posture of salutation before the mouth, while the syllable *hūṃ* is uttered with a fierce expression.
2.3.77 Preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, [the *guhyā-mudrā* is formed] at the secret place...
The Secret Place [41v]
The *kambojī-mudrā* consists of placing the two hands palms-upward upon the seat.
Regarding this, since not all the mudrās for perfumes and so forth have been mentioned here, that which was taught in the *Dvādaśasāhasrikā* is stated:

Extending the fingers of the "moon-hand" and raising them in a gesture of understanding, while grasping the "sun" with the whole [hand], this is the conch mudrā, which is like a conch shell: *oṃ supriyagandhe hūṃ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the fragrance mudrā.
Having joined the two hands in a hollowed *añjali* and turned them upward, one should cast [the flowers].
*Oṃ śrī svāhā~*. This is the mantra of the flower mudrā. Having formed two *vajra-muṣṭi*s, one should hold the junction with the moon.
Oṃ i svāhā~. This is the mantra for the incense mudrā.
Having formed the "sun-fist" (sūryamuṣṭi), one should place it upon the head of wisdom.
Oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā~. This is the mantra for the lamp mudrā.

2.3.78. Furthermore, according to the sequence here, there is another way: "The *praṇava* [oṃ] at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end of the [mantras] ending with *antānām*. This means the *hūṃ* syllable is preceded by *oṃ* and followed by *svāhā*. "Extending the hand for all" means extending both hands; this is the mantra for the *gandhamudrā* in reverse order. 2.3.79. "The *amṛtā*, the *repha*, and the *bindu*": *Amṛtā* is the letter *sa*; *repha* is well known as the letter *ra*. Both of these are joined with the *bindu* (the nasal dot), resulting in *oṃ*.
% [The reading *oṃkāra* is supported by the corrected version of the manuscript (MS\pcorr), while *oṃkākāra* is found in the uncorrected version (MS\acorr).]
[The mantra] ends with *svāhā*. [The mudrā] of the outstretched fragrance (*prasāritagandha*) is pressed by the thumb; thus, it is *krodhā tathā~*. The mantra for the flower-mudrā (*puṣpamudrā*) is:

"In the one preceded by the first of the classes" (*vargapūrvakapūrvasya*). "Preceded by the class" refers to the pair of initial vowels; that which is preceded by that is the vowel *i* (*ikāra*). [Thus the mantra is: *oṃ svāhā*.
Regarding the heading *°svāhādy°*: "In this case, one should apply the mudrās and so forth. This refers to the flower-mudrā (*puṣpamudrā*), wherein the thumb is placed in the middle of the hands.
The thumb. (Note: *ṅguṣṭha* emended from *ṅguṣṭha*)
Having thus joined [them], the mantra for the incense mudrā is as follows:
"Navāntābīja saṃgṛhya. This refers to the eight letters *ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa,* and *ha*. Their end is the ninth, the letter *kṣa*, which is preceded and followed by the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
"Having made a fist, raise the thumb"— this refers to raising the thumb of one who has formed a fist; it is the mantra for the lamp mudrā (*dīpamudrā*).

2.3.83–84. Regarding “the first group-triad”: the first group is the collection of *kalās*. Among them, the triad is the vowel *i*, joined with the nasal (*anusvāra*) and the bindu. It begins with *oṃ* and ends with *svāhā*. The mantra for the offering-gesture (*upahāramudrā*) consists of repeatedly moving the two thumbs between the two outstretched hands in the shape of a hollowed palm (*añjali*).

2.3.85. Regarding “one should worship them with these according to their reality” (*tatvena*): by means of this reality of the offering-gesture mantra, one should worship—that is, please—all the deities of the maṇḍala. What is the name of this [mantra]?
If it is argued that [the word] "Bali" [is used here], he says: "ādvaitya," and so forth.

"From the beginning," etc.: non-duality (*advaita*) is the absence of duality between the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, as previously stated. "Foremost" means superior to other offerings (*bali*). Since it was said that the mudrā and mantra constitute the *bali*, but not the substance to be given, he speaks of the substance: "five substances," and so forth. The five substances are those pertaining to the body; the five goads (*aṅkuśa*); and the five external meats.

2.3.86. He states another set of requisites for honoring: "flowers, incense, and so forth," and so on, up to "one should employ the mudrās and mantras. This refers to the mudrās prescribed for the *bali* offering for the purpose of consecrating it as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
The two mantras should be employed with the ten substances. After the nourishment with nectar (*amṛtāpyāyana*), he describes the worship, beginning with "twenty," etc.
(viṃśatyādi).

If it is asked, "How will one perform this worship consisting of twenty [verses]? he says: *hūṃkāra* and so forth. The syllable *hūṃ* is to be sung in the form of a song. He states the purpose: *sarvayoginī* and so forth.

All those *yoginīs* are pleased by this and become bestowers of boons; thus he shows that this [song] must indeed be sung. He states the instruction for singing it, beginning with "Vajramuṣṭi" and so forth. A fist as firm as a *vajra*, characterized by a *vajra* and a bell, is a *vajramuṣṭi*. Holding two of those fists at the two sides of the waist—[saying] "Hūṃ tṛ suṅga."

Regarding the term *cālayan* ("moving"): the three limbs are the navel, the heart, and the throat. By moving them—that is, by pronouncing [the syllable] in each of those places—the *hūṃ* syllable exists in its three states of protracted (*pluta*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*); this shows that it is to be sung in this manner. Its purpose is worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
% %\footnote{abhyudaye \emend] abhyudayo } % %
It is said: "By the *pluta* [vowel] there shall be liberation; the *dīrgha* [vowel] is traditionally held to bestow nourishment."
"Even by means of a short [mantra], one shall become subjugated," and so forth.
2.3.108 That [city], preceded by a self-constructed form consisting of the syllable *hūṃ* in the shape of a song (*gītikā*).

Having described the worship, he speaks a hymn of praise beginning with *vajjaü suraa*. *Vajjaü* means "let him sound. *Suraa-samattha*, meaning "heroic in sexual union" (*surata-śūra*), refers to one who is addicted to play consisting of song and other such forms. *Loaṇa-daṃsaṇae*: "loka" means the world; those people therein are the "eyes" (*loaṇāḥ*). [The purpose is] for the sake of being seen by them, who are thus to be instructed.
For the sake of seeing; for the delight of the letters; the nature of the existence of syllables; for the playful manifestation of the void.
2.3.109 Liberation from existence and non-existence: liberated from both existence and non-existence. To be understood through the middle way: for the sake of understanding the middle.
Having broken all syllables, for the sake of the cessation of reflection upon the remainder.

2.3.110 *dondāliṅgaṇajou*, the application of the conjunction of pairs (*dvandva*) and embracing (*āliṅgana*). *saalāvajjiae*, for the sake of winning over all (*sakalāvarjana*). *dhammu adyaita*, dharma has come today.
Having thoroughly attained this non-dual Dharma, even liberation is thoroughly attained.

2.3.111 *Suha saṃsāra vimohia* means: having deluded—that is, liberated—the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) by means of bliss arising from song and so forth; even liberation, as well as attachment to liberation, is abandoned for the sake of attaining that bliss. By means of the nature of all things—namely, the nature of song, dance, and so forth, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and objects (*viṣaya*). *Joiṇī* is an address. Alternatively, it means that by the five Yoginīs themselves, like mantras, the benefit of sentient beings is performed in many ways through dancing.

2.3.112. If one asks, "What would happen to the Blessed One during the dance of the five yoginīs within the [fivefold] interval? he says: *pañca vi joiṇi buddhatattva*, etc. The four yoginīs beginning with Vajraḍākinī, with Jñānaḍākinī as the fifth, possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the five Buddhas beginning with Vairocana. Does the Blessed One, who is the single remainder of all, become fivefold? [43v] No.

If one asks why, he says: "By means of *māyā*, he becomes multiform," and so forth. If one asks for what purpose, he says: "In order to ripen sentient beings" (*sattaü pāciae*). This is for the sake of ripening sentient beings who possess various inclinations, in accordance with their respective inclinations.
2.3.113. Regarding that which the yoginīs avoid: "The body is also a task" (*sārīa kajja*). If one asks why, he says: "Because they are deluded regarding the Dharma," and so forth.
% \footnote{°vimohiae ityādi \emend] °vimohiaevetyādi } %

Since the Dharma is bewildered and obscured by preoccupation with cause and effect, if one asks, "What indeed should we do then? he says: "Prostrate to the excellent essence, the Dharma," and so forth. This is the Buddha’s speech at the time of his enlightenment: "Prostrate to that Dharma which is the true essence, by which sentient beings are liberated."

2.3.114. By means of this six-line verse ending with these [words], Vajrapāṇi also offered praise out of devotion for the Blessed One who had been extolled by the yoginīs, beginning with: "Homage to you, O Lord of Yoga, Liberator of Beings," and so forth. Yoga is that which has the nature of the mantra, its configuration, and the Dharma; the Lord of that is the one who reveals it, and his address is "O Lord of Yoga" (*yogādhipa*). He is called the "Liberator of Beings" (*satvamocaka*) because he releases beings bound by the snares of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Because he is the source of the three realms of existence...

Because he is the source (*prabhava*) of all things, he is "the father of all existents" (*sarvabhāvātmaja*). Because he cuts through the two positions of existence and non-existence, he is "the one who brings about a single state of being" (*ekabhāvaka*).
[The reading is] °bhāvaka, as corrected in MS\pcorr; MS\acorr reads °bh+ + ti.
when it ought to be stated, [it is stated] by way of a single nature (*ekabhāvata*).

2.3.115. Because it is difficult to fathom, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is like an ocean; thus, "the ocean of cyclic existence" (*saṃsārārṇava*). Delusion (*moha*) is the notion that one is attached to that [ocean]. Its remover is the "Cutter of the Delusion of the Ocean of Cyclic Existence" (*saṃsārārṇavamohacchedaka*). The five principles (*tattva*) are the five families (*kula*); his body is the dissolution of those, hence he is the "Sole Principle" (*tattvaika*).
[44 recto] O Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, homage to you! Thus, with the sound of the vajra-bell and the rhythmic clapping, he sings this hymn accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ*.

2.3.118–119. Immediately following the praise, he states the *mudrā* in order to perform the vow (*praṇidhāna*) explained at the beginning of the *Abhisamaya*: "The vajra-palms," and so forth. It has assumed the form of suchness (*tathatā*) by virtue of its indivisibility.

The body, speech, and mind are the *vajra*; its manifestation is the five Buddhas in the form of the *añjali* (clasped hands). Having firmly formed such an *añjali*, having grasped it, and having made it stable, one should hold it in the "place of the heart," that is, in the heart itself. This means having acted in such a way that it does not slip again. And it is said: \begin{verse} ... \end{verse}
The triple-reality is indeed the vajra; the añjali-gesture consists of five deities:
Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

Thus it is said. Alternatively, "vajra" refers to that which is as indestructible as a diamond due to its extreme density. "Añjali" is the hollowing together of the two hands. Having placed that añjali at the heart, one should make this aspiration:

2.3.123–125. To show the *mudrā* for the purpose of focused concentration (*praṇidhāna*), he says: "The *kamalāvarta*" and so forth. Just as a lotus awakens through the impulsion of the wind, the dancing of the two hands with their fingers extended is the *kamalāvarta*. From the *kamalāvarta*, the right and left hands become a fully blossomed lotus and a vajra. Reciting the mantra "Ha Ho Hrīḥ," one should display these great *mudrās*.

2.3.126 "And everywhere for yogins"—that is, the Goddess everywhere, in all directions. He says this in order to show that she should be visualized not only among all the goddesses, but elsewhere as well:
"the worldly [goddesses], and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the worldly" (*laukikādim*) and so forth: the worldly ones are the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*). The supramundane ones are the sixteen heroes (*vīra*). Regarding the phrase "the outer maṇḍala is imagined": one should show [the deities] starting from the nine goddesses within the inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*), then the twelve goddesses who uphold the rampart, the four goddesses at the corners, the sixteen heroes such as Lokottara, Karaṅka, Bhairava, and others on the outer terrace, and the gatekeepers and so forth stationed outside at the doors and corners.

2.3.127 Regarding "separately with fragrance": it is not the case that by worshipping one [deity], all become worshipped; rather, one should worship each deity individually with fragrance and so forth.

2.3.128 He also states the meditation and the mantra for the nectarification (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of the five substances and so forth mentioned immediately above: "The five nectars mixed," and so on. "Mixed" means combined. "The five substances. Regarding that, both the meditation and the recitation are taught: "The letter *ha* takes away the color," and so on. The three letters *ha*, *ho*, and *hrīṃ* take away the color, smell, and potency; they also take away the five innate impurities (*malas*), the five hooks (*aṅkuśas*), and the objects of the senses, intoxication, and so forth.
2.3.129 This triple mantra is "threefold," i.e., three times.
"Three times" means having uttered it three times; "one should cause [the disciple] to meditate with the three deities" means one should contemplate the triple form of the three deities.

2.3.130. Regarding that, he states the deity: "Padmeśvara," and so forth. Padmeśvara is Vāgvajra. "Rūpasuvarṇa" means having a form like gold; because his splendor is like that [of gold], he is "rūpasuvarṇakānti. Such a mass of brilliance, Vāgvajra, takes away color. He... [sa[45\recto]rvākāra°]... takes away color.

Because it washes away the stains of discursive thought, it is like water; cultivate it as "fragrant water" (*gandhodaka*). Because its brilliance is beautiful, it is "splendidly radiant" (*surocana*), that is, Vairocana. In terms of taste, there is vigor; like a diamond (*vajra*) or the *bodhicitta*, it is the "taste-diamond" (*āsvādavajra*). Because he prevails when that [diamond] is lost, he is the Lord of the Taste-Diamond (*āsvādavajreśvara*); he himself is Vajrapāṇi Akṣobhya, the "Lord of the Taste-Diamond, Vajrapāṇi. Thus, "by the three deities."

The three deities are the Vajra of Speech, the Vajra of Body, and the Vajra of Mind. By means of the "threefold"—that is, by color, fragrance, and taste—one should cause these three deities to be known, that is, awakened.

2.3.131. Showing that this instrument for the immortalization [of the body] is not merely this much, but that there is something else as well, he says: "And on the left hand, the moon... and so forth. On the left hand is the moon; in its center is the "syllable *ma*," which is the syllable of immortality (*amṛtākṣara*). And that is of two kinds: the letter *aṃ* and the letter *sa*. To the question, "Which of these two is this syllable? he replies:

"Omniscient" (*sarvavid*) refers to the leader of the group, the letter *a*, which is the beginning of the group, by virtue of being the sprout of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "The Omniscient One" is the Blessed Lord whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), free from conceptual construction; he is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*). By the word "by the mothers" (*mātraiḥ*), it is shown that this is not merely one [letter], but rather that which is surrounded by the entire collection of phonemes (*kalākalāpa*). "And on the thumb, earth itself" (131d): on the thumb located there, "earth" is the syllable of the earth-element, the letter *ha*. 2.3.132 "The ring finger... (*anāmā*)...

One should place the single [syllable] called *amṛtā* on the ring finger (*anāmikā*), specifically on the tip of the ring finger of Mount Sumeru. Regarding the word "by moving" (*calena*): by moving the two fingers—the thumb and the ring finger—upon which the syllables have been placed, one churns that nectar (*amṛta*) with water. This is done "three times."

2.3.133 He states what must be done: "One should cause the *cchiḍiṅga* and the thumb to be given. Having uttered the name for each respective deity, [one says] "cchiḍiṅga," [and performs] the snapping sounds (*cchaṭā*).

One should give. Regarding the phrase "afterwards by means of one's own being": one should cause the emanated and worshiped wheel of deities to enter into oneself—in the form of the aggregates, elements, and so forth—by means of the mind.

2.3.134. Next, he speaks of meditation upon the self, beginning with the words "pañcasphoṭikaṃ tu" and so forth. The four limbs are the phonemes *a*, *i*, *u*, and *e*. The vowel *o* is surrounded by these. These five Buddhas take the form of the five channels (*nāḍī*); that in which they burst forth is the "five-fold bursting," namely the throat. Regarding the word "of the stūpa": because it consists of the five Buddhas and the four goddesses condensed into a peak (*kūṭībhūta*), the heart is the stūpa. At the tip of the tongue is the *ūrdhvabindu-hūṃkāra*. Regarding the phrase "by the three places":
at the three aforementioned places, there is the *pluta*, the long, and the *hūṃkāra*.
Having meditated upon the *hūṃ* syllable as protracted, long, and short,
one should bathe and nourish oneself with solid foods, soft foods, and delicacies.

2.3.135–136. If one asks how this food or drink, which is nectar for the yogin or yoginī, should be given when being offered, he says: *pecchia*, etc. *Pecchia* means having looked at or observed. *Sohia* means purified or made completely pure. *Dhammu* means the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), having attained the state of perfect purity. *Lehi* means receive or take it.

Regarding *sambhāva* and *sambhāvya*: thinking "this is edible; how can it be eaten?"—[the text says] *na hi melu*, meaning "do not release [it]. If one asks, "If it is not to be released, what indeed should be done?", it says: *khaddhu*, etc. Because there is no distinction in being a living being, one should give [the food] saying, "Eat together with the Brahmins, dogs, and so forth."

2.3.137. Regarding the statement "He says [the deceased is] dead" while reciting "Kamalāvarta," etc.: "Kamalāvarta-pūrva" means having placed the pair of hands with the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā] first. "Cittasphaṭikacetanā" means that because it is stainless through the absence of stains such as stinginess (*mātsarya*), the mind is like a crystal; thus it is the "crystal-mind" (*cittasphaṭika*). Its consciousness (*cetana*) is exceedingly pure.

"Nirmalā" means with such an intention. Immediately after the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā], one should release and extend the left hand from the seat, holding the right hand as a three-pronged vajra—with the little finger pressed by the thumb and the remaining three fingers extended—and give it [to the deity].

2.3.138. If it is asked, "The giver gives by means of this [teaching], but by what does the recipient receive?", he says: *svāgadu dhammu*, and so forth. *svāgadu*: welcome (*svāgataḥ*). Because it is purifying and a source of merit. *dhammu*: the Dharma (*dharmam*). Because it brings about liberation (*mokṣāvāhana*). *aṇagghu*: priceless (*anargham*). *rāamalāgatae*: for the removal of the five stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as passion (*rāga*) and the rest, of the yogin. *gāhāgāhavivajjia*: free from the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakavivarjjitam*). *paṇavaha*: bow down (*praṇamata*).
Bow down with devotion.
2.3.139 *asya gāthene*ti: he takes it with this verse; having taken it, he consumes it.
He said:

"Consume it as its true nature. That is, consume it—that is, eat it—as its true nature, which consists of the nectar of knowledge. "Pure in everything," meaning that for the yogin, because of the purification by mantra, there is nothing whatsoever that is impure. Having said, "As you please," he consumes it.

2.3.141. At the conclusion of the meal, one offers the *bali* oblation. Regarding the phrase "with a red mandala" and so forth: one should fashion a small mandala with red pigment in the center of a triangular altar. 2.3.142. With the two little fingers interlaced and drawn by a white goad, and holding yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should invoke the outer deity.
2.3.143–144. *Oṃ kuru kuru samayādhipati hūṃ jaḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the invocation mudrā.

2.3.145–146. Regarding "with a red flower": one should offer a red flower, incense mixed with red [substances], and a sacrificial oblation (*upahāra*) to Bali. Regarding "the vessel for the oblation-offering" (*ohārabalibhāṇḍa*): those things which are offered are called *upahāras*, such as fish, meat, and so forth. The oblation consisting of these is the *ohārabali*. Its vessel is the *bhāṇḍa*.
"Bhāṇḍa" means a vessel for food; that which is brought here [is called] "upahāra."
[He] said: "Raw fish," and so forth. Raw fish, raw meat, and whatever is edible, such as fruits, roots, flour, *jambulikā*, and the like—these are offered in a vessel filled with them.
°pātre] MSᵖᶜorr, °pātrair MSᵃᶜorr
Placing [the vessel] in the left hand, one should display it over the hollow of the right hand.

Regarding the locations where [the deities] reside and those by whom they are to be worshipped, as well as the places and the worshippers, [the text says]: "Under a single tree," and so forth. The place extends as far as the *Mātaṅgas*. Kṛṣṇarudra and the others are the worshippers. "This" refers to these [deities], Kṛṣṇarudra and the rest. By the command of Vajreśvarī—that is, Jñānaḍākinī—one should invoke all of them and cause whatever rite is to be performed to be done.
It should be caused to be performed;
thus he says: *ka kka kaḍhḍhane*, etc.

2.3.156. All this ritual action is to be performed as follows; regarding that, he states the rule: “*Amṛte*,” and so forth. “*Amṛte*” means having filled the face with the radiance of nectar (*amṛtakānti*). “*Bhāvayed yogayoginī*” means: *yoga* is that which is joined (*yujyate*), such as [the practice of] *kakka*, *kaḍḍhana*, and so on. One should visualize her performing that very action for which she has been appointed within the ritual.
(Note: *amṛtakānti*!)

2.3.157–160. Having formed a pair of linked chains with the two ring fingers, and having bound two vajra-fists with their backs joined to one another, [one recites] the mantra beginning with *oṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa* and so forth. Regarding *yathākarma*: having kept in mind whatever rite it may be, such as pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and so on; regarding *bali bāhya tatvena*: outside the maṇḍala, externally, having prepared the offering (*bali*) by means of blazing, heating, and so forth, one should feed it.

2.3.161. Now, regarding "but the specific worship": specific worship is the pleasing of the circle of one's own maṇḍala deities. "Free from *kalpa* and *akalpa*": *kalpa* refers to the conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is edible" and "this is inedible"; *akalpa* refers to the lack of certainty regarding the [deities'] hooks (*aṅkuśa*) by virtue of their being deities. That which is free from both is "free from *kalpa* and *akalpa*."
Free from kalpas and aeons;
the fivefold reality of the five hooks.
Is it *pañcatattvatvam*? (The state of being the five principles?)

To determine [the meaning], he says: "The one named Mahāṅkuśa," and so forth. Mahāṅkuśa is the human; Jñānaḍākinī is the goad; Vajrāṅkuśa is the cow, Akṣobhya; Śvāna is Ratnasaṃbhava, the royal goad, the elephant, Amoghasiddhi; Cala is the horse, Amitābha. By means of this fivefold goad, which has the nature of the five Buddhas, one should please the entire circle of deities. He states the conduct for those practicing with the five goads: "But not those who delight in sensual pleasure," and so forth.
This [place] must not be frequented by jackals and the like who are dependent upon this body and life; indeed, it is not to be approached by them.
One must not practice [this] again;
likewise, those who delight in enjoyments must not practice even by consuming meat.
Those who delight in enjoyments should not practice [this].

2.3.165. If it is asked, "How indeed should one practice?", he says: "All according to one's own will," and so forth. When [the time] is obtained and when it pleases [one], then one should practice, and not by way of necessity. Regarding "in the midst of its seeds": that is, in the midst of those five goads (*aṅkuśa*); "of the seeds" means one should join the seed-syllables *āli* and *kāli*. 2.3.166. Through the application of that, by means of this which has become nectar, [one worships] all the deities...

One should satisfy all the deities. [With the mantra] "In the center, nectar indeed," one should consume [the substance] after having applied the imperishable nectar— the nectar flowing from the center of the mouth of the *vijñābhaṅgā* casket.
