2.3.167. "All remaining things" refers to the various items of food and drink that remain after being consumed by the members of the *samaya*.

"One should arrange the outer mandala" means that one should arrange [the offerings] for those situated outside the mandala, such as the laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*). If one asks how this is to be done, he says: "The *hūṃ* syllable in the form of a song. That is, by means of the *hūṃ* syllable in the form of a song.
[The reading] °ākāreṇa [is found in] MS\pcorr; MS\acorr reads °ākāreṇe...
"Filled with the sound of the maṇḍala" means [the sound] of the various songs, instrumental music, and so forth of the maṇḍala masters.
Accompanied by resonance.
Note: The remains of the *gaṇacakra* go to laypeople!
2.3.168–169ab. He states the subject matter: *paṇavaha*, etc. Prostrate before the one whose own limbs are the limbs of the heroine devoid of [worldly] emotion (*bhāva*).
(Correction:
*svāṅgāya*)

To him who is adorned with the illusory power (*māyā*) of the union of embracing the couple (*dvandvāliṅgana*), to the one whose garment is yoga (*yogāmbara*); having thus expressed the meaning, he utters the song: "HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ. From the sound of this song of the syllable *hūṃ*...
Uttering [the sound]...
% % something missing here %

He said: “*Vajraghaṇṭābhinādasya*,” and so forth. One should sing the *hūṃ* syllable while maintaining the rhythm of the sound of the vajra-bell. He states the measure: “*Sveccha*,” and so forth; one sings for as long as one desires.

Having thus [concluded], he says in order to make the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*): “*Vajrāñjali*,” and so forth. With the vajra-añjali firmly bound and placed at the heart, one shall make this aspiration: “*Sarve sattvā*,” and so forth.

2.3.172 He explains the dismissal (*visarjana*): "With the *vajramuṣṭi*, etc. Having applied the left *vajramuṣṭi* to the heart and placed the extended right fist on the ground, one should dismiss [the deities].
2.3.173 One should recite: "Oṃ, abide as the self, hūṃ svāhā.

2.3.174 "Afterwards, by means of the breath of the self": having established the wheel of deities within oneself by means of the wind of the breath and having worshipped oneself, one should dismiss the external deities and the eight guardians of the directions.

\paragraph{2.3.175–176} Having uttered: *oṃ sarvaduṣṭān gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gaccha gaccha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should dismiss [the deity] with three snaps of the fingers. \paragraph{2.3.col.} Thus ends the third chapter on the *parapīṭha* in the *Mitapadā-pañjikā* composed by Durjayacandra. ||oṃ||

[47v6] 2.4.1 Having explained the third chapter, he speaks in order to explain the fourth chapter, beginning with the words "I wish to hear," and so forth. [He asks about] the specific nature of the six [substances], such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five hooks (pañcāṅkuśā), Līlā, the conceptualization of non-dual phenomena (advayadharmavikalpana), and the external mudrās.
According to the system of the Yogaśāstra, what are these six [mudrās], such as vākyamudrā and so forth?
What kind [of person]?
Thus he asks.
2.4.4 Therein, regarding the states of being primary and secondary:
Is it because of their non-existence?

Having placed the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) at the forefront, the Blessed One spoke of the five nectars: "Listen, Vajrapāṇi, I shall tell you the reality of each one of them individually," beginning with "In the east, the nectar is vajra-water," and so forth. [This refers to] the nectar of all of them.
Of the nectars.

This is the subsequent *vajrāmbu*; that shall first be explained here. One should understand that this *vajrāmbu* consists of five natures. How is it that this single [substance] consists of five natures?

If one says, "I believe," [it is like] saying, "Fire is hot," and so forth. Since heat is perceived in this [object], it may be considered as fire because of its possession of heat; such is the case with touch.

Regarding the statement, "Wind is seen to smoke": for this fire, wind is perceived as the means for smoking—that is, for its flaming—because heat is impossible without wind, and because the sensation of heat is impossible in the absence of fire; thus, [the presence of] fire is established, like a flame.

2.4.5 *Apa dravabhāgam* ("Water is the liquid portion"). Water is perceived as manifest through its fluidity; thus it is "watery. It is also like earth because of its possession of form. *Jñānādhiṣṭhitavajreṇa* ("By the thunderbolt presided over by consciousness"): all this is presided over by space, which is the thunderbolt of consciousness. This [universe] consists of five elements.

He shows that this has been established: if one asks what should be done here regarding the fivefold vajra-water, he says: "Of the five deities," and so forth. One should contemplate the five seed-syllables of the five substances, such as fire and the rest, which are the purifications of wind and the rest, as well as those of Buddhalocanā and the other [consorts]. As it is said:
\begin{verse} ... \end{verse}
Apas is renowned as Tārā, Agni is Pāṇḍaravāsinī;
Vāyu is this awakened goddess Māmakī, and likewise Sundarī.

What has been established by this? This "vajra-water" is the nature of the five great elements in their condensed and unelaborated form; the wind and so forth are its elaborated forms. Therefore, [it is] the wind and so forth...
The non-duality of wind and so forth with the vajra-water.

2.4.6 Objection: Granted that wind and the other elements may exist within the water of the thunderbolt (*vajra*), but how can there even be the possibility of fire, which is contradictory to their coexistence? To this, he says: "The configuration of all [elements]" and so forth. He thinks as follows: if one were to know... [MS\pcorrsecunda, vidyāta MS\acorr] ...in this case.
Then fire does not consume even a single portion; therefore, this [fire] is also of the nature of fire.
And this too should be understood as follows.
It is to be understood; having thus [said],
the body [was addressed].

Now, in order to convey those seed-syllables (*bīja*) through a convention for the benefit of those who do not possess universal knowledge, he says: "Just as the wind," and so forth. "Just as" (*yathā*) indicates an illustration. "The wind" (*vāyuḥ*) refers to the letter *ya*. "Of the eternal ones" (*nityānām*) refers to the letter *ha*. "In the *haṃsa*" (*haṃse*) refers to the letter *sa*. "Earth" (*pṛthivī*) refers to the letter *ha*. "Witness" (*sākṣiṇa*) refers to the letter *kṣa*.

2.4.7 “Having joined [them] with the *bindu* and the *nāda*”: the *bindu* is the anusvāra; the *nāda* is the vowel *u*. These seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be joined with these two respectively. “And the five syllables of gnosis” (*jñāna-m-akṣara*).
[The word *pañcadhā* has been conjectured for *pañca ceti*.]

The syllable of knowledge is the imperishable syllable *akāra*, and it should be applied in five ways. If one asks where, he says: "In the middle there. "There" means in the middle of the seed-syllables of wind (*anila*) and so forth, together with the anusvāra. Regarding "the nectar-syllable in the middle of the moon," this nectar-syllable *akāra* should be seen as the bindu situated in the middle of the half-moon which has been transformed from that [anusvāra] *akāra*.
2.4.8 "It should be stated as 'five, five'": these are the five seed-syllables.
The seeds.

It should be stated that these are the five deities beginning with Anila. If one asks, "What is the purpose of establishing their status as deities? he replies with the words "Vajra-water, self-purification," and so forth. The meaning is that through the visualization of the forms of the deities within the vajra-water and within self-purification, there is the complete purification of the continuum of the yogin's own mind.

If one asks, "What would that which has been purified in this manner be like? he says: "Free from existence and non-existence," and so forth. "Existence" (*bhāva*) is the nature of the apprehended object; "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The meaning is that it is devoid of these two forms, resembling a reflection, and utterly pure. If one asks, "What would follow from this? he says: "Therefore, delusions are far away."

Because this is completely pure, delusion—characterized by loathing and so forth—is cast far away; that is to say, it does not remain. It should be understood that this very practice, when performed while free from delusion, necessarily yields its fruit.

2.4.9 Out of delusion, those who harbor doubts that this is merely another form of nectar [the five nectars] are told the following in order to demonstrate the equivalence of the five nectars with the well-known nectar: "The external nectar is the excellent substance," and so forth. The external nectar is cooked by provoking—that is, igniting—the fire, and this is well known in the world. However, as for what the five nectars are and how their production occurs, he speaks the following in order to demonstrate both of these points: "Saffron is gnosis, fire... and so forth.

Saffron is blood; gnosis is flesh; fire is the heat of the limbs; the "remnants" (ucchiṣṭā) are those left over after eating. Alternatively, they are "excellent remnants" (utkarṣeṇa śiṣṭāḥ), meaning fully ripened. Excrement is feces; the substance is adamantine water. As for the *bodhicitta*, it has been explained previously;
that is this very nectar (*amṛta*).
Like external nectar, the goad is cooked by the fire of knowledge. [As it is said: "The cooking by fire is for the fires. By fire...
Having cooked it with fire.

Having cooked that [nectar] and this [other substance], both are offered into the fire; thus, he demonstrates the equality of these two. Granted, there may be some similarity through the process of cooking and so forth, but in order to purify this "five-fold nectar" (*pañcāmṛta*) as something pure, he says: "By the seed-syllable of the vajra-lotus," and so on. "Just as for the eternal winds" (6c). One should perform the purification of the vajra-lotus, which is the *bodhicitta*, by means of the five seed-syllables already shown. If one asks how this is done, he says:
"And he should recite the seed-mantra" means that one should recite and consecrate these five substances with their respective seed-mantras, having placed the five seeds according to the proper rule.

Regarding the phrase "in the middle of that": one should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire called *kṣuṃ*, known as the "syllable of consciousness" (*ciccākṣara*), which is garlanded with flames, in the midst of this fivefold set of substances. Thus, it is shown that this nectar shall become pure, serving as the cause for Buddhahood.

2.4.12 Having prepared the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he now speaks in order to prepare that which is known as *amṛtakānti*: "Padmeśvara," and so forth. Because he rules over and has power (*īṣṭe*) within the lotus (*padma*) by stimulating passion (*mada*), he is "Lord of the Lotus" (*padmeśvara*). His form possesses a luster like that of gold, thus he is "Gold-Lustered Form" (*rūpasuvarṇṇakānti*). Water in which fragrance predominates is "Fragrant Water" (*gandhodaka*). And because he causes things to shine and illuminates them well, he is "The Illuminator of Existence" (*bhāvasurocana*).

He states the purpose [of the text] by asking: "Is it not sufficient merely through the practice of the nectar-like splendor (*amṛtakānti*), and what is the specific need for these particular qualifiers? He says: "Āsvādavajreśvaram," and so forth. *Āsvādavajra* is Amitābha; *Īśvara* is Vairocana; *Vajrapāṇi* is Akṣobhya. This triad of deities has as its essence the form of nectar (*amṛtākārātman*).

One should indicate by means of its form (*rūpa*). "By three kinds" means by way of being the Lord of the Lotus (*padmeśvara*), by way of possessing form, and by way of having the nature of water; that is to say, this purpose—known as the Radiance of Nectar (*amṛtakānti*)—is to be purified and then enjoyed.
2.4.13 Now he states its purification: "The letter *ha* removes the color," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
2.4.15 Now, in order to demonstrate the purification through the distinction between *ali* and *kali*, he says: "*Ali* is the bee," and so forth. *Aṃ* is *ātī*.

The companion says: "A *bhramara* is so called because it gives (*rāti*) wandering (*bhrama*), that is, roaming; thus, the connection is: 'They call her a *bhramara*, O companion. If one asks, "What is this *bhramara*? he replies: "The *bhramara* is Vajra and Bhairava. Thus, the *bhramara* is both Vajra and Bhairava. Not only does this term *ālī* apply to the *bhramara* as a synonym for Vajra, but in order to show that it also applies to the birth from Vajra—that is, to the birth from the birth from Vajra—he says: [the following].

"Empty as far as the limits of space"—this is said in order to exclude that which is not space, namely, unobstructed space. "By virtue of having the *dharmadhātu* as its intrinsic nature"—here, *dharma* is *tathatā* (suchness); that which holds these is the *dharmadhātu*. It is consciousness (*vijñāna*) empty of conceptual cognition; [the phrase means] by virtue of having that as its intrinsic nature.

2.4.16 It is not only that [the word] *bhramara* causes one to wander, but it also causes the referent, Vajrabhairava himself, to wander; thus, in order to make it understood that these two are difficult to comprehend, he says: “*Sakalotpannadehānām*,” and so forth. The meaning is: first, that in which the secret wisdom (*guhyadhī*) exists for the sake of the arising of the body of the Blessed One, who is endowed with all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). Furthermore, he states the reason for clarifying why this too is difficult to comprehend: [he says...]

"Of the eighteen channels," and so forth: having drawn up all this [world] into the midst of the nectar of the eighteen channels—[this side of the folio is slightly effaced; many readings are uncertain].
The sense faculty dissolves into the *āli* of great bliss. The meaning is that by these reasons, even if not explicitly commanded, one will necessarily come to know it.

Having established the *āli* along with its divisions, he speaks for the purpose of approaching it, beginning with "by the terrifying vajra-sound" (*bhairavavajranādena*). The instrumental case in "by the sound" (*nādene*) is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthe*). Thus, for the sake of the vajra-sound—that is, in order to play the vajra—he flew up terrifyingly.
% Huh?

\paragraph{2.4.20} \textbf{kālī}, etc.—A lotus flower that does not arise from mud and so forth is proclaimed as \textbf{kālī}. Because its nature is non-different from space, it is \textbf{devoid of physical form} (*vigrahavarjita*). Alternatively, because all disputes are pacified herein, [it is called *kāli*]. It is the cause of the arising of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the ocean of gnosis (*jñāna*).

2.4.21–22: Since water is the source from which knowledge arises, this Kālī is not only metaphorically described as the ocean; rather, in order to demonstrate that there is yet another excellence (*sāmyagrya*), he says: "With wisdom as the makaras and fish," and so forth.

The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in all phenomena is *prajñā*. And because all the sense-faculties are destroyed by it, as if by crocodiles and fish, *prajñā* itself acts like a crocodile and a fish due to this common characteristic (*sādharmya*). Therefore, this Kālī has *prajñā* as her cause; she is the abode of crocodiles and the like, and she is the ocean—this is the similarity between the two. Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the mud of non-duality" (*advayapaṅkamadhye*): the mud is like mud, hence "the mud of non-duality"; that which is in the midst of that is "in the midst of the mud of non-duality. When [it] is impelled by the sprout of skillful means (*upāya*), namely the vowel *Ā*, it blossoms.

In the lotus resembling the *bandhūka* flower—[regarding the term] "honey" (*madhu*)—that which is honey therein receives the name "immortality" (*amṛta*). [Regarding the term] "abode" (*ālaya*), it is its support, known by the name Kālī. "To that" means: this name Kālī belongs to that immortality. [Regarding the phrase] "the transformation is the flower, the water": having turned along the path of Kālī...
% Having turned around.
The meaning is that the term *madhu* applies not only to the flower but also to the honey produced from it.

(2.4.23) Having spoken of *āli-kāli*, he says this for the purpose of explaining the non-dual and dual-less Dharma: "the double-syllabled [mantra] previously extracted. Regarding the phrase "of that seed-syllable": it is called *akṣara* because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*) nor does it move (*na calati*). That which is both a syllable (*akṣara*) and a seed (*bīja*) is the "seed-syllable," specifically the one fixed as its deity, known by the name *kṣuṃ*. The "deity" of that seed is the "Mother of the Ritual Deposition of that Seed" (*tadbījanyāsakelamātṛ*).
"Having visualized the moon in the center"—that is, having meditated on the moon in the center. How so? "Visualizing the seed-syllable of Amṛtā"—that is, produced from the seed-syllable of Amṛtā.

2.4.25 Regarding the phrase "in the middle of what," he says, having proceeded even a short distance further: "of the machine arising from both. This means: in the middle of that which arises from both Āli and Kālī.
2.4.26 Regarding the phrase "just as [the third letters] of the classes," he extracts the seed-syllable of the milk-moon (dugdhendu). What is gained by this much?
This much has been demonstrated:
within the liquid moon situated in the midst of honey above the fire, there is a pair of excellent [syllables].
The two *sat*s [MS\pcorr; MS\acorr reads *mad*]. What is this?
"One should meditate on the seed-syllable of the milk-moon immediately thereafter," he says.

Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of extracting this?", he states the utility: "By these [syllables], the five nectars," and so forth. By means of these very seed-syllables—anal, amṛta, and the rest—the [substance] is thus purified.
The purified essence consisting of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) serves for the washing away of impurities and the purification of the body of "embodied beings" (*dehinām*), that is, of yogins.
2.4.28 “The gateways of the destinies” means the gateways of the sense-faculties according to their respective functions; from each of those [gateways], that [consciousness] also arises.

One should consume that nectar in this manner; enough with further elaboration. Regarding the phrase "of the very great sentence" (2.4.30a): that which has the word *mahā* at its beginning is to be understood as "great," meaning one who is not afflicted by diseases and the like. Thus, one who possesses these two words *mahā* is fit for consumption. Regarding the phrase "of the same class as the parched Vīraka": the *vajrī* is of the same class as this [substance] preceded by the word *mahā*. In that context, the "parched" (*cchuṣṭā*) are the four lower *gokudahā* seeds. Among these, the "heroes" (*vīrāḥ*) are those not impaired by old age and so forth—this is the meaning.

2.4.40 Regarding these, the seeds are, in their respective order: *hūṃ*, *huṃ*, *ghriṃ*, *jriṃ*, *śriṃ*. To show that these are not intended solely for the severing of delusion (*moha*), but also perform other functions, he says: "The ten substances," and so forth. [This refers to] the five nectars (*amṛta-pañcaka*).

These ten substances are [to be used] with the five hooks; preceded by one hundred thousand recitations of their respective mantras, they are to be employed with other substances according to the specific ritual action.
"They should be joined," as found in the MS\pcorr; "they are to be joined" in the MS\acorr. [This is easily understood.]

2.4.46–49. **Dūtī** refers to a female servant (*dāsī*). **Her activity** (*tatkarma*) consists of piercing (*vidhi*) and so forth. Desiring to cause her to perform that activity, he says this in order to accomplish the fourfold group of Yoginīs. The passage beginning with "under a single tree" (*ekavṛkṣasya*) and so on is easy to understand. **Pauruṣa** means one cubit (*hasta*) in measure. On a cloth (*paṭa*) measuring four cubits and more in width, one should visualize their forms and postures as painted there and recite the mantra. To what extent...? (The rest follows).

If it is asked, "Is the deity painted on the cloth exactly that size?", he says: "Twelve finger-breadths [in extent] when stepped upon," and so forth; [this refers to the deity] being stepped upon, that is, paralyzed.

Regarding the phrase "of the paralyzed [painting]" (stambhitasya), it refers to the connection with the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). As for "twelve thumb-breadths" (*dvādaśāṅguṣṭha*): this is stated with reference to a painting measuring one cubit (*hasta*). On a painting of one cubit, or half of that, the deities are twelve thumb-breadths in size.
Twelve [fingers] plus a thumb.
It does not exceed that; thus, it is two, three,
or four [hands].
It is easily understood that for the *pramāṇa* [type of] cloth it is one half of that, while for the deity it is [the other half].

(2.4.96–97) Regarding the phrase "if she is not accomplished by that rite": if that Yoginī should be unaccomplished (*asiddhā*) by the rites just mentioned—such as the recitation of mantras and the writing of the cloth—the [author] states what must be done in that case: "In the sacrifice of heroes" (*vīramadhe*).
In the midst of heroes; [emended from *vīramadhe* to *vīramadhye*].

"Should honor" means: [among] the heroes such as Karaṅka, Bhairava, Khaṭvāṅga, Rākṣasa, and so forth—*in their midst*, that is, *among the heroes*—one should "honor," meaning one should measure [them]. If it is asked, "How should one honor them? he says: "One should split them into pieces in the sky."

"By means of *khaṇḍena*" and so forth: one should divide [the object] into pieces as many times as there are heroes (*vīra*). If one asks "by what?", he says: "by those characterized by the blow of the syllable *jriṃ*. "Blow" (*ghāta*)...

[The word *ghātaḥ* (MS\pcorr) refers to the syllable *phaṭ*; *dredṛṃsārddhaṃ* is the half-syllable *dṛṃ*. Thus, this is the meaning: Having expanded [the mandala] together with the axe produced from the syllable *jriṃ*, if one asks what he should do, it says: "He should devour" (*bhakṣayet*). That is to say, he should eat the heroes. If one asks how he should do so, it says: "By means of the meditations on the seed-syllable *hūṃ*" (*hūṃkārabījabhāvanaiḥ*). He whose seed-syllable is *hūṃ* is *Hūṃkārabīja*, namely Vajradhara. By means of the meditation upon him, the yogin—having assumed the form of Yogāmbara manifested instantaneously—should eat; such is the meaning.
2.4.100 Having become perfected as female servants according to the stated sequence, they are indeed [those previously mentioned]. 52v1. e[tāś]...

Having performed their respective duties, those four yoginīs, desiring to go into the midst of the circle of yoginīs in their own retinue, praised the Blessed One with a single voice, saying: "He shines!
(sohaï)

It shines (*sohaï*); it is liberated; from this comes liberation (*mokṣam*). *Ṇakoddhu*: one whose anger is pacified. *Samaa ciṭṭha*: remain in the right moment (*samaye tiṣṭha*). For the sake of liberation from this—
For our liberation.

Abide in the *samaya*! Take hold of the staff set with rubies with your hand; having looked (*prekkha*), O Hero, release it, O Blessed One! You who deliver one from *saṃsāra*! We go (*yāmīti yāmaḥ*). Open the door to liberation!
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear," and so forth—this is the definition of the *mudrā*-speech (101b). It is called *mudrā* because it gladdens (*modyate*).

*Mudrā* is that by which a yogin or yoginī is gladdened (*modyate*); it is the symbolic sign of the commitment (*samayacihna*). *Vākya* is the speaking of the secret conventions of one’s own commitment. The meaning is that, through the sequence of practice for the four yoginīs just mentioned, the yoginīs—who have entered into union with any one of the four yoginīs beginning with Ḍākinī—will request to hear the characteristics of the *mudrā* and *vākya*, which are not within the sphere of ordinary people.
2.4.102. Regarding this, he speaks in order to show the *mudrās*: "To the right of the *yogins*, etc. [This means: to the right of the *yogins*; to the left of the *yoginīs*, on the left side.

2.4.103–104. "Having cast into the mouth," and so forth: the sequence for displaying the *mudrās* is that the *mudrā* whose characteristics are about to be described must be performed. He states what will be spoken regarding the *ḍākinīs* and other *yoginīs* who are marked by the *mudrā*: "Gho ghv," and so forth. Thus ends the fourth chapter on the *parapīṭha* in the *Mitapadā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) composed by the Great Maṇḍala Master Durjayacandra. ॐ ॐ ॐ ॐ.
3.1.1 \textbf{Bhagavan} (O Blessed One) [53r] Bhagavan.
"I wish to hear the definition of the characterized and the characteristics from others," and so forth— those for whom there are no others are "others" (*apara*).

The Tathāgatas are so called because they are characterized by those [other] characteristics; that which is to be characterized by them is the "characteristic of the characterized" (*lakṣyalakṣaṇa*). If one asks what that is, he says: "the four realities," and so forth. The reality of the four is the "four realities" (*catustattva*); it is the essential nature of the vajra, the bell, and the rest.

3.1.2 If it is asked, "How? Of what nature is this realization of the Tathāgata that we, who are dull-witted like ourselves, should know? he says: "It has the characteristic of crossing over from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
3.1.3 Therefore, this fourfold reality (*catustattva*) should be known as the crossing over the ocean of cyclic existence.
3.1.4–64 The rest is easily understood.
3.1.65–67. Even for one who has realized the characteristic of reality regarding the vajra, the bell, and the rosary...

Since the accomplishments (*siddhi*) described as the reality of the vajra, bell, and so forth do not succeed for one who has not realized the reality of gnosis (*jñānatattva*), he says the following in order to demonstrate that: "Listen correctly, O Great Vajra," and so on. Regarding "in the differentiation of gnosis" (*jñānabhede*), it means in a particular kind of gnosis; "not far" (*na dūraḥ*) means not at a distance. The meaning is that the accomplishments are right in one's hand. If it is asked, "What then is that undifferentiated gnosis from which this distinction arises? he says: "the statement concerning common gnosis" (*sāmānyajñānavākya*).
Thus,
it is precisely the statement regarding general cognition.
Indeed, that very thing.

If one asks, "Of what nature is that?", he says: *daityadaityetyādi*. "Duality and non-duality" (*dvaitadvaita*) refers to the state of being divided into two, namely the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. That which is "beyond" (*para*) that is "beyond duality" (*dvaitapara*), meaning it has duality and non-duality as its primary characteristic; that very thing is "beyond duality and non-duality" (*dvaitadvaitapara*) because of its commonality with knowledge (*jñānasāmānyāt*). If it is asked, "What is the fault in this commonality of knowledge, such that one should set this aside and seek the undifferentiated (*aviśeṣa*)? he says: *daityetyādi*. The word *daitya* [is used] because [the former] is not to be accepted (*anupādeyatvāt*).
It is called "trackless" (*apada*) because it does not deserve a track; that which is this dualistic cognition regarding all phenomena that are non-dual is an error.
The double moon.

Like the cognition of two moons [53v], by this [example], the establishment of an object is indeed not desired; rather, it is shown that what is established is a non-object (*anartha*). To demonstrate this, he says: "By yakṣas, asuras, siddhas," and so forth. By means of this dualistic cognition, having transmigrated through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) in the form of yakṣas, asuras, and the like, [one is] "like a sentient being" (*sattvavat*).
[The reading *sattvapacyavat* is conjectured; it may also be read as *sattvavat*.]

Thus, sentient beings are cooked in hell; therefore, this dualistic cognition is ignorance and should not be accepted. But surely, because of the variety of mental forms (*ākāra*), the reality of non-dual cognition is established precisely by this.

If it is asked, "Since [the deities] are established, from where do the accomplishments (*siddhi*) to be achieved by them arise? he says: "By means of canopies in the form of animals," and so forth. Regarding the word "animals" (*tiryañc*): starting from animals, those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are to be mentioned. These, moreover, are the hell-beings (*nāraka*), the hungry ghosts (*preta*), humans, the gods of the Four Great Kings (*caturmahārājakāyika*), and the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

The Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins; those belonging to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), namely the seventeen classes of gods beginning with the Brahmakāyikas who belong to the realm of form; and those belonging to the four bases of infinite space (catur-ānantaryāyatana) who belong to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). Regarding the phrase "because of supporting even the subtle egg" (*sūkṣmam aṇḍam api dhāraṇāt*): "subtle" refers to atoms (*paramāṇu*). "Supporting even the egg" means being covered by the egg, that is, situated within the egg.

3.1.69 “Presided over by omniscience” means that all this triple world, with its gross and subtle forms and so forth, is presided over by gnosis. Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*), this [world] is the locus of omniscience; therefore, one should not form an attachment to any real entity here. And it has been said:
The objects of the senses do not exist externally within the mind by way of their own nature.
"For it is mind alone that appears through the manifestation of form and so forth," and so on; there is also a statement regarding their distinction.
The manifold [world], characterized by non-duality, is constructed through the forms of the grasped and the grasper.
[The mind] abides precisely by means of those very [objects] that have been conceptually constructed.
[They] remained standing.
Thus ends the mind; this is the knowledge of non-duality.
[The word *jñānaṃ* is emended; it was originally *jñānaḥ*.]

The reality of knowledge (*jñānatattva*) has been stated. Now, one might ask: "If this non-dual knowledge is established, is ignorance (*ajñāna*) likewise established? To this he says: "Ignorance does not exist because it lacks effort. This means that so-called ignorance does not exist; "because it lacks effort" means because its purpose has already been exhausted. Therefore, all...

Saying "knowledge," he speaks while making [the meaning] understood: "Knowledge of all. This entire [world] has the form of knowledge. If one asks who says this, he replies: "The All-Knowing One" (*sarvavit*); the meaning is "the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*).

3.1.70 *Śrutaṃ kautūhalam*, etc. That non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*) which was expounded by the Blessed One has been heard and realized by me. Furthermore, there is a curiosity; I ask this: "By what is knowledge qualified? By what has this such non-dual knowledge been qualified—that is, rendered as if possessing differentiation? If one asks "Why?", he says: "Knowledge is presided over by the universal" (*sāmānyadhiṣṭhita jñānam*). Knowledge, acting as the agent, presides over the universal.
And that universal could not exist without particulars; since the universal is held to be precisely that which possesses all particulars, therefore the particular exists.
"I ask the Blessed One: by whom was this created?
Thereupon the Blessed One said: "Of the twenty and thirty gods," and so forth. The "twenty" refers to the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods; the "thirty" refers to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Trāyastriṃśas (the Gods of the Thirty-three)

Thus, for the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—beginning with those [of the Four Great Kings] up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods—who are greedy for sensual pleasures, there is a specific knowledge consisting in the cognition of external objects. [54v] Regarding the external [objects]: for those who perceive the five objects of desire as being external, there is "the knowledge of knowledge," which refers to the thorough knowledge of enjoyment. "Successively" (*ūrdhvaśas*): this knowledge of the fivefold divided objects of desire increases and accumulates further and further.

3.2.2 Regarding the phrase "of the wheel with nine squares," etc.: having drawn [the diagram] with a rim, a pericarp, eight petals, and a hundred petals, one should write in its pericarp the first two syllables [of the mantra], beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *hutānta* (svāhā), followed by the word *rakṣa* (protect) and the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*).
Having assigned [the syllables] for the *vidarbhaṇa* on the eight petals, the remaining [syllables]...
The remaining ones.

Having joined the eight syllables of the root mantra of the Noble Ārya Tārā Bhaṭṭārikā, each beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *huta* (svāhā), [one should place them] also in the compartments of the rim.
One should place the vowels beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *huta*.
[Regarding] "in the lunar mandala" and so forth: the lunar mandala...
The maṇḍala in the center.

Having visualized that lotus situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala, one should understand that one should perform this rite after producing oneself, standing upon that [lotus], in the form of a star through the application of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).

3.2.27–30. “Eight petals,” and so forth. This too is an eight-petaled wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*) with a rim and a pericarp (*karṇikā*), like the wheel of stars (*tārācakra*) on all sides. Here, for the purpose of interlacing the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the genitive case—ending in words such as “increase wisdom” (*prajñāvṛddhiṃ kuru*)—one should place the first two syllables beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *hūṃ* in the pericarp. On the petals, one should place the remaining syllables, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *hūṃ*. [The mantra is: **oṃ prajñe mahāprajñe hūṃ svāhā**.
Therefore, there are eight seed-syllables; likewise, there are sixteen on the spokes.
They are employed; however, the specific distinction here is the placement of eight *hūṃ* syllables even upon the filaments (*keśara*).

3.2.34 Regarding the phrase "of that which has a nine-square interior," and so forth: the inner chamber consists of nine squares, the middle chamber of twelve squares, and the outer one of sixteen. Having drawn such a wheel, complete with a rim on the outside, one should arrange the mantra therein.

3.2.35 If it is asked how this is done, he says: "In the center, within one's own mind," and so forth. In the center, that is, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*), is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, which is the wisdom-body (*jñānadhātu*) of oneself. "Of the eighth" refers to the eight seed-syllables beginning with *suṃ* in the eight inner squares. [He places] the twelve vowels, excluding the neuter ones, in the twelve squares.
3.2.36 "According to the third of each group" refers to the third letter of the three groups beginning with the *ka*-group.
The sixteen syllables of *takārādhika* [are to be placed] in all sixteen squares.
And all, indeed, all.
Having placed these letters beginning with *ka*, joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, in their respective positions, one should join those ending with *phaṭ* to the rims.

[3.2.42] Regarding the passage beginning with "of the solar disc" (*sūryamaṇḍalasya*), [the text says] "garlanded with shimmering rays. [3.2.43] He speaks in order to explain this seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the solar disc: regarding the passage beginning with "of the preceding group as it stands" (*yathāvarggasya pūrvasya*). Among the groups of consonants as they are established, the first group is the *ka*-group; its initial letter is the letter *ka*.

"3.2.44 ‘I am tormented by the goad’: having joined *ka* with the vowel *i*. ‘One should cause the root to have the letter *ra*’: one should join it with *ra* below. ‘The nectar-drop is above [the others]’: one should meditate on the head of the drop situated in the middle of the half-moon, which arises from the syllable of nectar."

3.2.46 Regarding the passage beginning with *dviguṇākṣaram*: the "double-syllabled" (*dviguṇākṣara*) is the syllable *kṣa*. One should join this with the vowel *u* below, the half-moon on top, and the bindu; one should then join it to the heart of the Yoginī. As for the phrase "this is named Amṛtāntika": the syllable *kṣuṃ*, ending in *sa* (i.e., *kṣuṃ*), preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and followed by *hutānta* (*svāhā*), is to be recited.

3.2.48 *pūrvalakṣaṇa sarveṣām* and so forth. *Pūrva* (previous) refers to the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) and the like. *Lakṣaṇa* (characteristic/sign) refers to worship, the confession of sins, and so on; as well as the previously mentioned emptiness (*śūnyaka*) and the like. "In that very [wheel] of gnosis and so on, just as it was described"—this refers to the departure for enlightenment (*bodhiprasthāna*), emptiness, and so forth. *Cintayed ātma sarveṣām* means one should contemplate oneself as these [qualities].

And one should contemplate all [these] in their proper sequence. If it is asked, "With what should one contemplate the Self?", he says: "By the measures of the All-Knowing Immortal" (*amṛtā sarvavitmātraiḥ*). Regarding "Immortal" (*amṛta*), this refers to the letter *sa*. This is the qualifier "by the measures of the All-Knowing" (*sarvavitmātraiḥ*). "All-Knowing" (*sarvavit*) means the Omniscient One. The eight syllables, beginning with *kṣuṃ-yum* and so forth, which bring about that [Omniscience], know everything; their measures (*mātrāḥ*) are the constituent parts of the syllables—the half-*u*, the bindu, and the nāda. These are the "measures of the All-Knowing."

By them this seed-syllable is perceived as consisting of that alone; because of its application, even the first vowel called *amṛta* is not grasped. Therefore, having assumed the form of the syllable *su*, one should manifest oneself in the form of Vasudhārā.

To demonstrate the application of this yoga, he says: "Of all those drawn in by the breath," and so forth. The meaning is that by means of the breath, whatever one desires of anyone, that very thing one draws in.

3.2.50–51. Regarding the phrase "of the bodies of the one to be accomplished" (*sādhyasya tu dehānām*): having visualized the body of the one to be accomplished as residing within the body of the solar disc; and regarding the phrase "the goad-syllable of the mind" (*aṅkuśākṣara cittasya*), one should encircle that mind—which is the syllable *i*—with the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyubīja*).
Thus,
one should contemplate [the deity] as having the syllable *yaṃ* at its core, within the aforementioned colors,
and so forth.

One should meditate on these two seed-syllables with the object of accomplishment as the third, all being red. If one asks, "What is the nature of this object of accomplishment, and what is the nature of the meditator? it is said: "Situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala," and so forth. And by the practitioner...
And [56v] blood.
The intended meaning is that one should become the form of the Emanated Wisdom-Ḍākinī (jñānaḍākinī) situated in the center of the red maṇḍala.

(3.2.52) If it is asked what the yogin will do even when he has performed the yoga of the Wisdom-Ḍākinī, it is said: "One should perform the mental attraction" (*manasākarṣa bhāvayet*). The meaning is that one should effect an attraction by means of the mind (*manaḥ-karṣaṇaṃ kuryāt*).

3.2.53 If it is asked, "How is this done?", he says: "The goad and the index finger are moved," and so forth. One should impel the goad held in one's own hand with the index finger. If it is asked, "What would result from this?", he says: "It brings about the realization of the syllable *Aṅkuśa*."

This is the meaning here: one should meditate upon the syllable *i*, which represents non-duality as it has been described, as being drawn by this goad. Regarding the phrase "of the double-syllabled [seed] and the bindus," the double-syllabled [seed] is *kṣuṃ*.

3.2.54 “This is the one named Amṛtāntika”: *amṛtā* is the syllable *suṃ*; since this name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) ends with that, it is called “the one named Amṛtāntika,” which is the syllable *kṣuṃ*. “It succeeds in the characteristic of subjugation” (*vaśalakṣaṇa sidhyati*): these two mantras possess the characteristic of subjugation; the meaning is that by means of them, subjugation is accomplished. If one asks, “In what manner? he says: “By these, [it] is made known” (*ebhir jñāpita*).

Regarding the phrase "of entities" (*bhāvānām*): by means of these two syllables *kṣuṃ* and *suṃ*, preceded by the visualization of the heart of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the name of the one to be accomplished is to be recited in a *vidarbha* (interlaced) manner.
[Verse 3.2.55] "One should encircle the rim of the eight-petaled wheel on the outside. This means that outside the rim, [one should encircle it] with the syllable *ṃ* and the letter *ṭha*.
By the very letter ṭha.
One should encircle it. Regarding the rule "the depression (*nimnakā*) [is] for all vowels": one should encircle the depression between the two rims with all the vowels.

Regarding the rule "the first syllable of the fifth class according to its group": having joined the letter *pa* with the letters *i* and *r*, one should place it "in the middle," that is, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

3.2.57 *saptamādasya yojya* (to be joined with the seventh sound). From the vowel *a*, the seventh sound is the vowel *ṛ*; that is to be joined (*yojya*), meaning it should be applied. If one asks where, he says: *dalāsevanaṃ tu kārayet* (one should cause the service of the petals). *Sevyaṃ* means to be served; it refers to the four petals in the directions starting from the east. The meaning is that one should join [the sound] there. If one asks what else is to be joined in the intermediate petals, he says: *pañcamasya tu vargasya* (of the fifth group), and so forth. The third letter of the fifth group is the letter *ba*. One should employ that here.

3.2.58. If one asks what this wheel should do, he says: "One should visualize [it] as having the color of gold," and so forth. One should visualize it—filled with many rays of flame resembling highly refined, supreme gold—as being upon each and every body that is to be favored. 3.2.59. If one asks who is the visualizer, he says: "By the previously mentioned characteristics," and so forth. By those shown hereafter and above, [one perceives] non-existence through the emptinesses of all things.
The meaning is that the yogi is one who has accomplished the *vasudhārā*-yoga immediately following all phenomena (*bhāva*).

3.2.60 Not only is this wheel to be visualized, but it is also shown that the mantra located therein must be recited; thus he says: "In the center of the previously mentioned seed-syllable," and so forth. Having placed the three seed-syllables mentioned for the wheel in the middle of the *praṇava* offerings and the final [syllables], one should recite them.
3.2.61 If one should ask, "What is the purpose of this visualization and recitation? he states the objective: "The yoga of nourishment" (*pauṣṭika-yoga*).
Yoga is accomplished.
3.2.63 *sūryamaṇḍalamadhyastham* and so forth—by means of the sun, fire, and moon of Kālī. Regarding *jñānavijñāna*: one should contemplate either two *hūṃ* syllables or one.

3.2.64 If it is asked where those very sun and moon are to be seen, such that this seed-syllable is to be visualized within them, he says: *dalāṣṭacakrasya madhya* and so forth. This means in the center of the sun and moon disks situated upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of an eight-petaled wheel.

3.2.65 Having visualized this wheel as having its exterior encircled and its rim depressed by being joined with the vowels beginning with *a*, he speaks for the purpose of depositing the seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon the petals: "Four nectars in the directions. This means the four syllables of nectar, namely the four *suṃ*s, in the four cardinal petals. "Combined with all mantras" means [the sequence] beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *hūṃ*. "But four in the intermediate directions" means the four *hūṃ*s in the intermediate petals. And that very [wheel] is adorned by the five Buddhas. As for the expression "five Buddhas," it is mentioned in various places.

3.2.66–71. Regarding the phrase "one should contemplate one's own body": one should visualize within one's own body the eight-petaled wheel filled with the seed-syllable of one's heart. Regarding the phrase "the full moon-maṇḍala": this is stated so that one may visualize this wheel as having come into being in such a manner. The passage beginning with "situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala" and so forth is easy to understand.

3.2.72 Regarding "the *mahāmudrā* is with both hands": he says that the *bodhyagrī* mudrā is to be bound with both hands so as to press upon the heart, stating, "pressed against the location of the heart. 3.2.73 Having removed the three seed-syllables from this very wheel by means of the yoga of Mahāvairocana, he says "trembling," and so forth, in order to show that wisdom (*prajñā*) is also to be meditated upon. Regarding "trembling" (*sphurantīm*), [the word] *bhā*...

Regarding the phrase "of various sharp things" (vividhatīkṣṇānām): because it burns the fuel of all ignorance, one should contemplate this wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*) as being sharper even than all other objects of a sharp nature that exist in various forms. He states the purpose: "in the world-transcending" (*jagottare*), meaning it is the cause for delivering the world. If one asks what that wheel of wisdom is, he says: "of the seed-syllable preceded by the vowels," and so forth. The vowel-preceded seed-syllable is the letter *a*; and that is accompanied by the visarga (*aḥ*). It begins and ends with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and the oblation (*hūṃ*).

3.3.1 *Śrutakautūhalaṃ deve* and so forth. Regarding the sequence of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānakrama*) and the procedure for entry (*āveśanavidhi*): "I have heard" means that there is a desire to hear. "By which the cultivation of the yoga of empowerment was shown to sentient beings" means that by means of this sequence of empowerment which has been shown, through the application of yoga, faith is produced in sentient beings who were previously skeptical, and their minds are established in the maṇḍala circle of the pledge (*samaya-maṇḍalacakra*) and so forth.
The meditation on the yoga of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānayoga*) occurs through the application of [the ritual] installation (*āropaṇa*).

3.3.2 When Vajrapāṇi requested, "Tell me, then, what is that like? the Blessed One said: "Listen, O Vajra, according to reality," and so forth. "According to reality" means as it is clearly manifest. "The perfect essence" (or "the cycle of existence").
For those individuals who are destined for the unsurpassed means; furthermore...

Furthermore, [the text] confirms that very point: "He should teach the dharma of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to beings who possess doubt. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) means uncertainty or censure. He teaches the dharma through empowerment to those beings for whom that [doubt] is predominant; the sense is that they cannot be disciplined in any other way.

If it is asked how this empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is accomplished, he says: "Having visualized the moonlight in the heart," and so forth. It is called *candrika* because the moonlight (*candrikā*) has arisen within it;
[it is thus a lunar disk].

Having visualized the maṇḍala and the syllable *hūṃ* situated in its center—[described as] "divine with the radiance of blazing fire"—the term *agnijvālaprabhādivya* means that which sports (*divyati*) by means of those radiances (*prabhā*), that is, the flames (*jvālā*) of fire (*agni*). The meaning here is that this syllable *hūṃ*, having approached the ten directions in the form of the radiance of blazing fire, sports there together with the world-systems (*lokadhātu*).
3.3.4 What kind of thing is this for them, moreover?
Again.
If it is asked, "Is this the sporting of those belonging to the world-systems?", he says: "All, all are destroyed," and so forth.

They are exhausted—that is, they are led to exhaustion—by their own inherent nature in every single way. If one asks by what means, he says: "by those belonging to the world-systems of the ten directions," meaning by those situated in the world-systems located in the ten directions. If one asks how this is done, he says: "having visualized the circle of fire," and so forth.

Having correctly visualized the circle of fire in the manner described, the blazing of that fire within all locations—including mountains, trees, atoms, and all entities categorized as inferior, superior, or middling—is "the blazing of all locations."

3.3.5 He shows that they are exhausted in such a way that not even one remains; if it is asked, "What should one cause him to do?", he says: "Endowed with the previous characteristics," and so forth. Yogāmbara—[referring to Āryadeva and others].

*Pūrvādiḥ*: "Previous" refers to the *bodhicitta*. Its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is its essential nature (*svarūpa*); that which is endowed with this is "endowed with the previous characteristic. *Pūrvaśūnyādi*: first, one should cause—that is, generate—the *bodhicitta* of setting out (*prasthāna-bodhicitta*), such as the enclosure (*prākāra*) and the cage (*pañjara*). If it is asked, "When those world-systems of the ten directions have been burned, what form does one see of the burning *hūṃ* syllable? he says: "Situated in the center of the fire-maṇḍala," and so forth.

Because there is no possibility of anything to be burned, it is withdrawn; that which is situated in the center of the circle of fire is "situated in the center of the circle of fire. If it is asked: "While other seed-syllables such as the double-syllable (dviguṇākṣara) and so forth exist, which are capable of accomplishing the act of burning, how is it that this single syllable *hūṃ* alone was obtained by the Blessed One? he says: "The five Buddhas, however, have contemplated [it].
O Vajrapāṇi, do not understand this merely as a mantra; this *hūṃ* is the five Buddhas, the five Buddhas...
Because it consists of parts that are distinct [and] because it is composed of the five Buddhas.
3.3.6 If it is asked, "Who [is] where?", he says: "The staff is the lord of the worlds," and so forth; this is easily understood.

3.3.8 To show that the expansion of ritual action (*karmaprasara*) succeeds only when its presiding deity is fixed, and not when it is without a deity or when its deity is otherwise fixed, he says: "In the center of the solar disc," and so forth; this is easily understood. (emended to *°madhyastham*)

3.3.11–13. Regarding the phrase "of those that are third in their respective groups": the seed-syllable of the milk-moon (the letter *va*) has been mentioned; one should recite it three hundred thousand times, beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *svāhā*. Having offered the *bali* according to the prescribed rule, he speaks on how to begin the induction (*āveśana*). Regarding the passage beginning with "of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) combined," etc.: one should give food and drink prepared by the method of consecrated pills (*gulikā*), which have been empowered by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over the five nectars combined. To whomsoever one gives this, he becomes possessed at that very moment. This makes him fit (*bhavyīkaraṇa*).
For the purpose of making [beings] capable [of liberation].

3.3.14 He addresses him, who is thus possessed like Vajrasattva, in order to urge him on with a vajra-song: "Rama rama ho vajja tuhum," and so forth. "Kīḍa kīḍa" means "play, play. "Vajja tuhuṃ" means "you, O Vajra-holder! "Savvasamattha" means "capable of accomplishing all siddhis. "Kheddu" means "to be consumed. "Tuhuṃ dīaṇu" means "you, being given"; "dāaṇu" means "the giver. "Joḍa" refers to the recipient.
Even for one who is practicing yoga, there is the consumption [of food]; you are thus Vajrasattva, [and] *mahuṃ* means "me," [and] *saṃsāra*.
*Tāru*: deliver from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). *Khaṇu*: in an instant.
(3.3.15) Thus, accompanied by the sounding of a bell and the brandishing of a vajra, having realized his own state as a Vajradhara, he dances, sings, and meditates out of great joy.

3.3.17 “He should satisfy all of them with that”—by means of that nectar, he nourishes the heroes and yoginīs situated within the maṇḍala. “He should show”—he should demonstrate such a capacity. “There, the Dharma is to be performed”—in this context of the rite of possession (*āveśana*), for disciples who have attained either a slight, partial, or perfect possession—whether they be inferior, middling, or superior—he must reveal the Dharma according to their respective spiritual capacities;
he shows that it must not be done otherwise.
3.3.18 Just as this [medicine] effects the entry of a non-poisonous spirit— what? [It is] *āveśa*.
And in order to demonstrate both the possession through mantra and the possession through vision, he says: **Oṃ yogāveśa aḥ**.
And so forth. These two types of possession are to be understood through this very perspective.

3.3.33 Regarding the empowerment for protection and so forth: demonstrating the efficacy through this beginningless protection, he says: "Having recited it seven times," and so on, which is easy to understand.
Thus ends the third chapter on the Yoga-pīṭha in the Mitapadā Pañjikā composed by Durjayacandra. ॐ.
3.4.1 Curiosity (kautūhala)

The heading: *Kautūhalaṃ śrotum* (Curiosity to hear). [This refers to the passage beginning with] "Having become curious to hear the non-dual yoga (*advayayoga*), [he asks] ‘from what essence (*sārata*)’; [and] ‘the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the non-dual statements. How is this non-dual statement designated as “non-dual”?

3.4.2–3. Let it be granted that the statement regarding non-duality (*advaya*)—like a flower in the sky and so forth—is indeed devoid of a referent (*nirabhidheya*). If it is asked, "How then should one undertake the practice of that non-duality (*advayayoga*)?", he says: "Listen, O Vajra, how correctly... and so forth. The meaning is: "Listen to that non-dual yoga according to reality (*tattvataḥ*)."

"Vajra is reality (*tattva*)," meaning that by way of reality, the vajra is the self, the body of the yogin. "Bell is the Dharma," meaning by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). The bell is the deity, the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the yogin. The union of the two seals (*mudrā-sampuṭa-yoga*) is the "seal" (*mudrā*). Regarding "the means (*upāya*) dissolves into it": in that union of the two seals, the couple consisting of that means dissolves and is no longer perceived. To grasp this triad within the accomplishment of non-duality, he says: "The vajra, the bell, and the seal," and so forth.

\paragraph{3.4.4} If one asks, "How so? it is said: "First of all," and so forth, which is easy to understand. \paragraph{3.4.8–10} With the water that washes away the stains of the grasped and the grasper, the three purifications establish the wall of generosity (*dāna*), the cage of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the pegs of patience (*kṣānti*).

\paragraph{3.4.12} Regarding the phrase "with the fragrance of the mind of equanimity" (*samatācittagandhena*): the mind of equanimity is the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*); that itself is the fragrance, like the fragrant substances of saffron, agallochum, musk, and so forth. By means of that fragrance of the mind of equanimity...

Having smeared [the ground] on all four sides with the auspicious [mudrā], one asks: "What is this 'equanimity' (samatā)? It is said: "Of those whose bodies are [treated with] the axe and sandalwood" (*vāsīcandanadehānām*). Those whose bodies are [subjected to] the axe (*vāsī*) and [anointed with] sandalwood (*candana*) are "those whose bodies are [treated with] the axe and sandalwood" (*vāsīcandanadehāḥ*); [it refers to] those for whom there is a killer with the axe and one who anoints with sandalwood. That state of consciousness which remains equal is "consciousness established in equanimity" (*samatāsthitacetanā*). Because it is non-dual, that very thing is expressed by the word "equanimity" (*samatā*).

3.4.13 Because it is the antidote to impatience through one-pointedness of mind, patience is called *dhyāna*. *Dhyāna* depends upon the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). That is twofold: pure and impure. To specify that very [pure *dhyāna*], he says: "Of that which is pure by nature," and so forth. The object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is pure by nature—that is, pure by its own essence (*prakṛti*). With the incense being offered to that object of meditation which is pure by nature, there is non-duality and equality; that itself is the cultivation of incense, the "cultivation of incense as equality" (*samatādhūpabhāvanā*).
3.4.14 *Prajñā*, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); that itself is the lamp, the island of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-dvīpa*).
By means of that lamp of wisdom, having illuminated and made light of the triple world, one should destroy the darkness of ignorance that obstructs the path.

(3.4.15) At the beginning of the phrase "providing no consolation," etc., one should console sentient beings by means of the gift of fearlessness, characterized by the bodhicitta of engagement, in the manner described above.
3.4.16–17. One should practice by visualizing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) in locations that are pleasing to the mind.
He states what is to be done: "Having fully accomplished that 'the vajra is the self'... and so forth.

If it is asked, "Having emanated wisdom (*prajñā*), what should one do next?", he says: "With equal vision" (*samadṛṣṭi*), and so forth. "Equal vision" is the non-occurrence of [discrimination] regarding all phenomena. "Form" (*saṃsthāna*) is the perfection of shape and appearance. "Consisting of the nature of a person" means being endowed with all the excellent marks of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Regarding "meditating on the syllable *hūṃ* in the heart": meditate on the syllable *hūṃ* in the heart of either the vajra or the bell; this is easy to understand.

3.4.19 “Situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala”: because it indicates unimpeded gnosis, it is situated within the interior of the moon-maṇḍala located in the middle of the peaked pavilion; thus, it is “immovable.
Emerging from the drop of the syllable *hūṃ*, produced from the drop of the syllable *hūṃ*.

3.4.21 Regarding the phrase "in the form of Vajrasattva and so forth": one emanates oneself in the form of the two-armed Vajrasattva and others. If one asks how this is done, he says: "One should place the arrangement of syllables," and so forth; this is easy to understand. This "formation" (*kalana*) is well known through the eight seed-syllables. Showing that there are nine, including the syllable *hūṃ*, he says: "The formation of the syllable *hūṃ*," and so forth; this is easy to understand.

3.4.30. To show that not only the syllable *hūṃ* is to be meditated upon, but that recitation (*japa*) must also be performed, he says: "When the *āli* and *kāli* have been extracted," and so forth. This means [the mantra] has been extracted—that is, separated—from the *āli* and *kāli*. 3.4.31. Furthermore, to demonstrate the meditation on this immortal syllable (*amṛtākṣara*), he says: "The *sattva* for the crossing over of the *liṅga*," and so forth. *Sattvaṃ* means of beings (*sattvānām*); *uttāra* means in the act of crossing over; *liṅgaṃ* means the cause. Thus, *sattvam uttāra-kāraṇam* [means] the being that is the cause of crossing over.
The meaning is that it is both to be recited (*japya*) and meditated upon (*bhāvya*); this is the reason for its being called *uttāra*. Now...

If it is asked, "By whom should this being (*satva*) at the tip of the bell—the mark of the *uttāra*—be visualized?", he says: "By one whose hand is placed upon the embrace" (*āliṅganyastapāṇinā*). This means by the yogin who holds the *vajra*, with his hand engaged in the act of embracing. Regarding the phrase "of the *vajrāṅguṣṭha*" and so forth: because it is intent on threatening the wicked, the thumb is like a *vajra*; thus it is the *vajrāṅguṣṭha*. The finger is the index finger (*pradeśinī*). At its tip, at its peak (*śikhare*)...

3.4.32 “But one should show [it] on the left side. Because desire (*kāma*) is by nature left-handed (*vāmaśīla*), one should show the goddesses the syllables of nectar (*amṛtākṣara*) contemplated at the tip of the index finger of the left hand. If one asks how this is done, it says: “held at the front. The meaning is that it should be such that the remaining part of the arm embraces her neck from the front.

3.4.33. If it is asked, "Is the accomplishment of the goal achieved by the mere sight of the finger? he says: "Moving [it] on his forefinger," and so forth. "Of him" refers to those eighteen places of nectar. With that forefinger, one should impel—that is, awaken—the unawakened nectar. If it is asked, "When is this arousal of desire to be performed? he says: "Having abandoned the embrace of the couple," and so forth. "Couple" (dvandva) means sexual union; "embrace" (āliṅgana) means a close hug.

Out of steadfastness, having not yet made this non-duality manifest before him— [the phrase] "facing the east" means facing the vajra— he should "place it," that is, he should cause it to remain stable.

"Apply the yoga. "For the sake of all beings" (*saalākajjiae*), meaning for the purpose of all sentient beings and not for the attainment of one's own self-interest. If it is asked what kind of yoga that is, he says: "Beginningless" (*aṇāhī*), and so forth; it is beginningless because it has no prior limit. If it is asked why it is such, he says: "By the Yoginī," and so forth; since she "devours" (*ādya*) the Yoginī by means of this [yoga], therefore it is beginningless. This is the meaning here: the propitiation of the Yoginī is not the fruit of minor merit or austerity; that [fruit] is accomplished by this [yoga].
